title: The thumb push cut
subtitle: The primary controlled-removal cut in whittling
excerpt: The thumb push cut is the core stroke of whittling. It uses the thumb of the knife hand as a lever point to control stroke length and depth. Once it becomes automatic, it replaces most other cut styles for fine work.

glossaryTerms.definition: A leather strap charged with abrasive compound, used to maintain a sharp edge between honings.

content.text: The thumb push cut is a short, controlled forward stroke in which the thumb of the knife hand presses against the work and acts as both a pivot and a brake. It removes thin, precise shavings in a direction away from the body. What makes it the primary whittling cut is control: the thumb limits stroke length mechanically, so an inadvertent forward slip of the blade stops at the thumb rather than continuing into the other hand.
The cut is used for all fine shaping, for removing ridges, for approaching a marked line, and for any cut where the depth and direction need to be held precisely.
Before you start cutting.
Grip: four-finger grip on the work; thumb-push grip on the knife. Never make a cut whose blade-path can reach a body part.
Cut direction: the thumb push cut goes away from the body. Never adapt it into a pulling motion toward the body.
Sharpening: a dull tool is more dangerous than a sharp one. The dull tool slips. Strop every fifteen minutes of carving, hone weekly, oilstone monthly.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
The grip

Hold the knife in the dominant hand with all four fingers wrapped around the handle. The thumb of the knife hand rests on the flat face of the blade, 2 to 3 cm back from the tip. The thumb is not on the cutting edge. Hold the work in the other hand with the work face pointing away from the body. The thumb of the knife hand presses against the surface of the work just ahead of the planned cut.
The stroke

The drive comes from the fingers: close the knife-hand fingers while pressing the thumb forward against the wood. This pivots the blade forward over the thumb contact point and into the wood. The shaving peels off ahead of the blade and the stroke ends when the thumb comes to a natural stop against the work surface. The maximum stroke length is roughly the width of the thumb, about 2 cm.
When to use a long-arm push cut instead

The thumb push cut works for fine work and short distances. For rough shaping and bulk removal, use a long-arm push cut: grip the work firmly on a chopping block, set the blade on the surface, and push the knife away from the body along the grain with the full arm. There is no thumb control here; the safety comes from the direction (away from the body) and the chopping block holding the work. Switch to the thumb push cut when the rough work is done and fine control is needed.
Common errors
Thumb on the cutting edge: the thumb must be on the flat spine side of the blade, not the edge. Check your grip before every session until it is automatic.
Too much blade depth: if the blade enters the wood more than 2 mm, the stroke is too aggressive. Shallow angle at entry, then tilt down only slightly.
Dull edge: a dull edge requires force to enter the wood. That force removes the control that is the whole point of the thumb push cut.
Strop
before starting any precision work.
Practice exercise

Take a 30 cm length of 25 mm square pine. Round it to an octagon using the long-arm push cut along each face. Then switch to the thumb push cut to take the octagon to a round cylinder. The transition from octagon to round using only thumb push cuts requires 40 to 60 controlled strokes. Done cleanly on pine without tearing, it confirms the grip is right.
